claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial rents for subdivided units.
Hong Kong should tighten security of tenure instead, with at most a light band on starting rents.
The stable SDU stock under the 2021 ordinance is not evidence that a binding cap is safe.
The stable stock shows that a non-binding instrument does not bind.
First-generation hard caps cause consistent contraction, while second-generation increase caps have small or null effects.
Long-run supply elasticity for marginal SDU-type stock is 0.31 to 0.48, so a 10% cap-induced rent cut removes 3-5% of stock over five years.
A 15% cut in initial rents transfers about 900 dollars monthly to incumbents while 3,000-4,000 households per year cannot enter the segment.
The households excluded by a cap are the same population that D1 identifies as the segment's core tenants.
Berlin shows that caps bind differently on entrants than incumbents, with the bill handed to those still outside.
Tenure security addresses the harm tenants actually name, which is insecurity rather than price.
Mr Chan says he would accept any rent to leave if the public-housing queue fell from five and a half years to three.
An NGO survey of 440 households found 61% would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74% for a faster housing offer.

The Landlords Association's threat of mass exit is weakly evidenced because it concedes no data on actual margins and its compliance-cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34% response rate.
The exit threat is credible for hard caps but not a reason to avoid limits on rent increases.
The NGO report is written by a group that wants tenure security, so it is not relied on alone, but the academic paper reaches a similar view on hard caps.
Rent burden for these households worsened from 31% to 34%, and figures after 2023 rely on survey extrapolation, so doing nothing is not enough.
A hard rent cap would help those who already have a unit and hurt those trying to get one.
Tighter security of tenure gives tenants what they say they want without the supply loss.

cites.sentence: The stability of SDU stock under the 2021 ordinance, 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 [D2p1], is not evidence that a binding cap is safe.

The working paper is explicit: first-generation hard caps show consistent contraction; second-generation increase caps show small or null effects, "which explains the stable stock in the D2 index" [D6p2].
One think-tank piece cited in the news digest makes exactly the wrong inference from this data [D12p2].

The academic literature estimates long-run supply elasticity for marginal SDU-type stock at 0.31 to 0.48: a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

A 15 percent cut in initial rents transfers about 900 dollars monthly to incumbents while 3,000 to 4,000 households per year, "mostly new arrivals and newly formed households," cannot enter the segment at all [D6p4].
That is the same population D1 identifies as the segment's core tenants [D1p2].
Berlin reinforces the point: caps bind differently on entrants than incumbents, and "the bill is handed to those still outside" [D7p3].

Mr Chan says the worst part is not price but insecurity, a landlord ending his tenancy with two weeks' notice [D3p1], and that he would "accept any rent to leave" if the public-housing queue fell from five and a half years to three [D3p3].
